newsitem.title: GERMANY: D.Telekom sees higher 1997 profit - CFO.
newsitem.headline: D.Telekom sees higher 1997 profit - CFO.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG will show a strong increase in profit in 1997, and meet its commitment to pay a 60 pfennig dividend for 1996, chief financial officer Joachim Kroeske said.

In an interview with Reuters Financial Television aired on Wednesday, Kroeske said he stood by an earlier projection that the company would show operating earnings of more than six billion marks ($3.7 billion) in 1996.
"Employee reduction is ahead of plan. Debt reduction is ahead of plan. Sales in 1996 were a little higher than expected. We will come to a strong increase in our profit in 1997," Kroeske said.
"We are looking for the same performance or better than other telecommunications companies."
On Monday, Telekom released data on its 1996 sales and said earnings were higher than expected.
"We will fulfil the six billion marks (operating profit), and we will be higher. But I am not able to say now how much," Kroeske said in the RFTV interview.
Kroeske said the 1996 results would justify its pledge to pay a 60 pfennig dividend, and that there was a strong increase in profit in the second half compared with the first half.
In an effort to lure retail investors to its new shares, last October Telekom said it would pay a 60 pfennig dividend for 1996, and double it to 1.20 marks in 1997.

Telekom reported 10.3 billion marks in group income from ordinary activities in 1995, down from 11.2 billion marks the year before, but these figures are not adjusted to reflect the impact of value-added tax payments it is now required to pay.
The company is expected to present a new set of 1995 data adjusted as if VAT were paid in order to present a comparable basis to 1996.
Unconfirmed German press reports last spring, citing internal Telekom documents, said operating profit was projected to rise to 10.3 billion marks in 1997 and to 16.3 billion marks by the year 2000.

Kroeske said he was not disappointed with Telekom's share price development since the initial offering at 28.50 marks in November, even though the shares dropped to a low of 29.82 marks last week from an interim high of 34.10 marks.
The shares were trading at around 31.15 marks at midday Wednesday.

"I would not say disappointing," he said. "We are now in the neighbourhood of a 10 percent increase from the initial price. In the last two months, there has been a positioning of the share price, in the DAX, and in comparison with all other companies.
Standard market benchmarks such as cash-flow multiples or dividend yields justify the initial offering price of 28.50 marks, which was not at the top of the expected range, he said.
After the initial settling-in period, Telekom shares should equal or outperform the DAX's performance, he said.
"I am happy if we reach around about 10 percent, and after a certain period, if it is two or three months, that we go on with the DAX, or better. That is our benchmark."

Monday's announcement of 1996 sales data was not made simply to boost the sagging share price, but showed that Telekom is ready to keep investors informed of developments as soon as reliable information is available, Kroeske said.
Telekom expects no insurmountable difficulties facing the renewed competitive challenges presented when Germany fully opens its telecommunications market in January 1998, he said.
"We have competition in Germany in mobile (telephony), in the fixed-link network, with local companies, with callback services. We see that we can manage this process."
"We expect that despite losing some market share we can increase our sales. By increasing our sales while reducing our costs, this will lead to an increase in profit."
Despite growing speculation that the European Commission could force Telekom to spin off its national cable television network, Kroeske said he does not expect that to happen.
"We do not see that we have to divest the cable TV network. The network is an important building block in our multimedia strategy."
Telekom is also looking for new opportunities abroad, including Japan, he said.

"Japan is one of the most important telecommunications markets in the world. It was nearly closed up till now. Now there is movement in that country, and we follow that. We will take our decision to take part in that region."
Telekom, which already has major U.S. and European partnerships, is looking for Asian partners. "We think we see a chance to fulfil that."
($ = 1.643 German Marks)
